subject: Cues per unit time per area to density of clusters/individuals in R Distance package

messages.author: 54c94f7c2bf78491
messages.subject: Cues per unit time per area to density of clusters/individuals in R Distance package
parts:
Section 9.4 of Buckland et al 2015 gives a good theoretical explanation of converting from cues per unit time per area to density of clusters/individuals. 

How is this done practically in the R Distance package? I don't see any arguments in the ds() function. Whilst I assume you could scale manually using a cue rate, I'm not sure how to deal with the confidence intervals produced by ds() when doing so. Vu et al. 2017 do something very similar in their paper A distance sampling approach to estimate density and abundance of gibbon groups, but using Distance for Windows.

For more details on my specific case: I wasn't involved in survey design, but I am analyzing point count data from gibbon groups, surveyed for around 5 hours each morning for 3 days from a number of sampling points. Distances to calling groups are estimated without triangulation. I have produced detection functions using the call data. Ideally I would use a cue rate from the literature, or calculate a cue rate from this data, and use that to adjust.

messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Cues per unit time per area to density of clusters/individuals in R Distance package
parts:
Good morning Olly

There have been enhancements to the R package Distance that incorporates the use of multipliers, necessary for use with cue count surveys.  The actual coding enhancements take place outside the function ds() .  The job of ds() is to fit detection functions, which is still needed to produce density of cues.  It is in a subsequent calculation where density of cues is converted to density of animals producing those cues.

Install a newer version of Distance

remotes::install_github("DistanceDevelopment/Distance")
and take a look at the exercise Sections 4 and 9 found here

I understand that the survey has already been completed, however, it is best to produce an estimate of cue rate (and its associated precision) at the time of the cue count survey, rather than lifting a cue production rate from the literature.
